fact:brief.text:
# binaries-lock.sh list: show what binaries.lock pins

## Problem
`scripts/binaries-lock.sh` can `check` the shape of `binaries.lock` and `fetch` one binary, but nothing prints what the lock pins. To see which versions of the temporal CLI and the test server are pinned, and for which platforms, you have to read the raw six-column rows.

## Change
Add a `list` command to `scripts/binaries-lock.sh`:

- `scripts/binaries-lock.sh list [--file F]` prints one line per pinned name, sorted by name: the name, its version, and the platforms that have a row, comma-separated in sorted order. For example: `temporal  1.9.1  darwin-arm64,darwin-x64,linux-arm64,linux-x64`.
- It reads the same file `check` reads (`--file` overrides the default `binaries.lock`), skips comments and blank lines, and writes nothing.
- Exit 0 when it printed; 2 on usage or I/O error (a missing file), the same as the other commands.
- The usage text in the script header names the new command.

## Done when
- `bash scripts/tests/binaries-lock.test.sh` has cases for `list` on the real lock (one line per name, the four platforms) and on a fixture with a missing file (exit 2), and passes.
- `scripts/binaries-lock.sh check` behaves as before.

items.text: When a person runs 'scripts/binaries-lock.sh list' with no --file, the script shall read binaries.lock and print one line per pinned name, sorted by name, each giving the name, its version and the platforms that have a row, comma-separated in sorted order (on the real lock: 'temporal 1.9.1' and 'temporal-test-server 1.39.0', each with darwin-arm64,darwin-x64,linux-arm64,linux-x64), and exit 0.
When 'list' is given '--file F', the script shall read F instead of binaries.lock and shall skip its comment and blank lines.
If the file 'list' would read is missing or unreadable, or 'list' gets an argument it does not take, the script shall exit 2 with a message on stderr and print nothing on stdout.
While 'list' runs, the script shall write no file and create no directory.
When the script prints its usage (no command, or a bad argument), the usage text shall name the 'list [--file F]' command and still end with the Exit line.

When a person runs 'scripts/binaries-lock.sh check' or 'fetch', the script shall continue to behave as before: same output, same exit codes, and 'bash scripts/tests/binaries-lock.test.sh' passes with its new 'list' cases.

fact:questions.question: How should 'list' separate the three columns on each line? The brief's example shows two spaces ('temporal  1.9.1  darwin-arm64,...'), but the real lock has names of different lengths (temporal, temporal-test-server), and the test has to match the exact text.

options.answer: Pad the name and version columns to the widest value plus two spaces, so the columns line up (the binaries.lock rows are aligned the same way).
options.rationale: Readable for a person, matches the lock's own layout and the brief's example on the 'temporal' row.
options.yields: AC-1 names aligned columns: name and version padded to the widest value, two spaces between columns.

options.answer: Exactly two spaces between columns, no padding.
options.rationale: Simplest to produce and to assert; matches the brief's example literally but the columns don't line up.
options.yields: AC-1 names a fixed two-space separator.

options.answer: One tab between columns.
options.rationale: Easiest for scripts to split (cut -f), but differs from the brief's example.
options.yields: AC-1 names a tab separator.

fact:questions.question: 'list' reads but does not validate (shape problems stay check's job). What should it print when the file gives one name two versions, which check reports as BIN-LOCK-003?

options.answer: Print one line per name and version pair, sorted by name then version, so the conflict is visible and the exit is still 0.
options.rationale: Keeps 'list' a faithful view of the file without validating it, and hides nothing.
options.yields: An AC: a name with two versions prints two lines, one per version, exit 0.

options.answer: Run check first and refuse (exit 1, pointing at 'check') when the file fails it, as fetch does.
options.rationale: Never shows a misleading view of a broken lock, but makes 'list' useless for looking at a broken one.
options.yields: An AC: a lock that fails check makes 'list' exit 1 with a message on stderr.

options.answer: Leave it unspecified: the real lock always passes check, so no case is needed.
options.rationale: Smallest change; the behaviour on a broken lock is whatever the code happens to do.
options.yields: No new AC.

fact:questions.question: What should 'list' do on a readable file with no rows (only comments and blank lines)? check fails it as BIN-LOCK-005; the brief says 'exit 0 when it printed'.

options.answer: Print nothing and exit 0: an empty lock pins nothing, and listing nothing is not an error.
options.rationale: Consistent with 'list reads but does not validate'.
options.yields: An AC: a file with no rows prints nothing and exits 0.

options.answer: Print 'binaries-lock: no rows in F' on stderr and exit 1, like check's BIN-LOCK-005.
options.rationale: Reads the brief's 'exit 0 when it printed' literally and flags an empty lock.
options.yields: An AC: a file with no rows exits 1 with a message on stderr.

options.rationale: AGENTS.md lists every command of the script; leaving 'list' out makes it stale.
options.yields: An AC for the AGENTS.md line, and AGENTS.md moves from unmapped into the scope.

options.answer: No: the script's usage text is enough, as the brief says.
options.rationale: Keeps the change to the files the brief names.
options.yields: AGENTS.md stays out of scope, listed as unmapped with that reason.

behaviours.question: Does 'list' refuse '--dest' and a bare '--file' with exit 2 (by a list-only parse, or by fixing the shared parser so 'check --file' also exits 2 instead of 1), or does 'list' keep today's shared parsing and AC-3 narrow to the missing-file case?

behaviours.text: I3 says 'list' prints whatever rows the file has without validating, but the output is one line per name with one version: a malformed lock where one name has two versions (BIN-LOCK-003) has no single version to print.
behaviours.question: When a name has rows with different versions, does 'list' print one line per (name, version) pair, print the first version seen, or refuse (exit 1, pointing at 'check')?

behaviours.text: The brief says 'Exit 0 when it printed', and 'check' fails a file with no rows (BIN-LOCK-005). A comments-only or empty lock gives 'list' nothing to print.
behaviours.question: On a readable file with no rows, does 'list' print nothing and exit 0, or exit 1 like 'check''s BIN-LOCK-005?

behaviours.text: The brief's example separates fields by two spaces ('temporal  1.9.1  darwin-arm64,...'), but the real lock's names differ in length (temporal, temporal-test-server), so the lines either keep fixed two-space separators or pad the name column; AC-1 does not say which, and the S6 test must match one.
behaviours.question: Are the fields separated by exactly two spaces, or aligned in columns (name padded to the longest name)?

behaviours.text: I3 says 'list' prints the rows the file has without validating, but a row with fewer than three fields (what check reports as BIN-LOCK-001, e.g. 'temporal 1.9.1') has no platform, or no version, to print. Taken literally it prints an empty column, which AC-1 ('no trailing space', padded columns) forbids, and no acceptance item says what happens.
behaviours.question: When a row has fewer than three fields, does 'list' skip it, print the fields it has (and if so, how do the padded columns look), or refuse (exit 1, pointing at 'check')?

behaviours.text: A file can list the same (name, platform) twice (check's BIN-LOCK-004). AC-1 and AC-5 say the platforms 'that have a row', comma-separated and sorted, but not whether a duplicate platform shows once or twice ('linux-x64,linux-x64').
behaviours.question: When a (name, version) has two rows for the same platform, does 'list' print that platform once (deduplicated) or once per row?

behaviours.text: AC-5 sorts by name then version, and AC-1/AC-2 sort names and platforms, but neither says which order: plain byte order puts '1.10.0' before '1.9.1', and a 'sort' left on the user's locale can order names with '-' differently on macOS (Bash 3.2, BSD sort, header line 13) and on Linux. The S6 tests compare exact text, so the order has to be the same everywhere.
behaviours.question: Are names, versions and platforms sorted in byte order (LC_ALL=C, so 1.10.0 comes before 1.9.1), or are versions sorted numerically by x.y.z while names and platforms use byte order?

walked.name: input: --file paths (missing, directory, unreadable, empty, malformed rows)
output format and ordering (padding, locale, duplicates, two versions)
portability (macOS bash 3.2 and BSD awk, Linux mawk and gawk)

behaviours.text: 'list --file DIR' where DIR is a directory: the script's guard '[ -r "$file" ]' passes for a readable directory, so the outcome is left to awk. mawk (this box) prints 'awk: read error (Is a directory)' and exits 2, but gawk warns that the argument is a directory, skips it and exits 0 with no output, which looks like AC-6's empty-file case (exit 0, nothing printed). AC-3 says only 'missing or unreadable', so the result depends on which awk is installed.
behaviours.question: Should 'list' (and the shared --file guard) treat a path that is not a regular file, such as a directory, like a missing file: exit 2 with 'binaries-lock: cannot read F' on stderr and nothing on stdout, whatever awk is installed, with a test case for it?

surfaces.title: scripts/binaries-lock.sh
surfaces.detail: Add the 'list [--file F]' command: one line per (name, version), sorted by name then version, giving the name, the version and the comma-separated platforms that have a row, each platform once; every sort in byte order (LC_ALL=C), the same on macOS and Linux; columns aligned (name and version padded to the widest value, two spaces between columns, no trailing space); skips comments, blank lines and rows with fewer than three fields; reads but never validates; writes nothing. Exit 0 when the file was read (an empty lock prints nothing), 2 on a missing or unreadable file or an argument 'list' does not take ('--dest', a bare '--file', a positional). The shared flag loop stays as it is for check and fetch; list's refusals are checked for list only. Name the command in the header's usage text; usage() prints the header by a fixed line range (sed -n '4,12p'), so the range must follow the longer header.

implications.text: usage() prints the script header by a fixed line range (lines 4-12); adding the 'list' usage and its description lengthens the header, so the range must grow with it or the usage text cuts off the exit line.

'check' and 'fetch' keep their arguments, output and exit codes: install-deps.sh, sindri-app.sh, CI and several tests call 'fetch', and ci-changed-areas routes on the script's path; none of them call 'list'.

'list' reads but does not validate: it prints the rows the file has, and shape problems stay 'check''s job (BIN-LOCK-00n). A name with two versions (BIN-LOCK-003) prints one line per version, a file with no rows (BIN-LOCK-005) prints nothing and exits 0, a row with fewer than three fields (BIN-LOCK-001) has no platform to report and is skipped, and a platform listed twice for one name (BIN-LOCK-004) shows once.

The flag loop is shared: '--file' with no path dies through ${2:?} with exit 1 and '--dest' is accepted by every command ('check --file' exits 1, 'check --dest /x' exits 0). 'list' refuses '--dest' and a bare '--file' with exit 2 by a check of its own, so check's and fetch's parsing, and their exit codes, do not change.

The interview closed with no answers, so the column layout (AC-1), the two-version case (AC-5), the empty case (AC-6) and the AGENTS.md line (AC-10) follow the recommended options Q1.a, Q2.a, Q3.a and Q4.a; an answer that picks another option changes those items.

Three places describe the script's commands besides its own usage text: binaries.lock's header (S5), AGENTS.md's Commands block (S8) and docs/csharp/sindri-workflow.md (S9); each gets a 'list' line so none goes stale.

The S6 tests compare exact text and the script runs on macOS (Bash 3.2, BSD sort) and Linux, so every sort 'list' does (names, versions, platforms) runs in byte order under LC_ALL=C; versions are not sorted numerically, so '1.10.0' comes before '1.9.1'. Only a lock that fails check (BIN-LOCK-003) has two versions of a name, so the order of those lines needs to be fixed, not clever.

The second challenger round's three behaviours (a short row, a duplicate platform, the sort order) came after the interview closed, so AC-13, AC-14 and AC-15 take the choice that keeps 'list' a plain, validation-free view of the file: skip what has no platform, show each platform once, byte order everywhere. A person who wants otherwise (refusing a short row, numeric version order) changes those items.
